blocks: After Gallus and Volusianus the son of Decius, the rule of the Romans passed, according to most, to Valerian and Gallienus his son. When those two had been done away with by the treachery of their own army, as was said before, these held the same rule for 15 years; but according to some, Aemilianus stood at its head for a period of three years, and when he too was done away with, by Valerian's design, the same Valerian was declared emperor of the Romans.

Under Valerian and Gallienus the Scythians crossed the river Ister again and plundered Thrace, and besieged Thessalonica, the Illyrian city, though they achieved nothing there, thanks to the courage of its guards. Alarmed at this, the Greeks guarded Thermopylae; the Athenians then rebuilt their wall, which had been pulled down since the time of Sulla, and the Peloponnesians walled across the Isthmus from sea to sea; and the Scythians went home with much plunder.

On top of this Shapur, king of the Persians, overran Syria, came to Antioch, and laid waste all Cappadocia. When the Roman army went hungry at Edessa and was thrown into disorder by it, Valerian took fright, and pretending to go out to a second battle he gave himself up to Shapur, king of the Persians, agreeing besides to betray the army; but the Romans saw it and barely escaped, a few being killed. Pursuing

blocks: them, Shapur, king of the Persians, took Antioch the Great, and Tarsus of the Cilicians, and Caesarea of the Cappadocians. Then the Persians, scattering out of greed, some here, some there, and on the point of taking Pompeiopolis by the sea, and ravaging Lycaonia, were killed in great numbers, when Callistus, the Romans' general, whom the fugitives had put at their head, fell on them unexpectedly with ships and a force. He also captured Shapur's concubines, with much wealth, and moved with the fleet to Sebaste and Corycus, where he killed three thousand Persians. Grieved at this, Shapur turned back in haste and fear; and Valerian remained among the Persians to the end of his life.

Odenathus of Palmyra, a man of military gifts, fighting as the Romans' ally, destroyed many of the Persians as they were going back, falling on them in the region of the Euphrates; and for this he was honoured by Gallienus as general of the East, after he had also destroyed some of the Romans who had risen against him in Phoenicia.

Then again the Scythians, who are called Goths in their own tongue, came by the Pontic sea into Bithynia, and overrunning all Asia and Lydia they took Nicomedia, the great city of Bithynia, and destroyed the Ionian cities, catching some unwalled and others only partly fortified; and they even reached Phrygia, ravaging Troy, Cappadocia and Galatia. But Odenathus, after his successes against the Persians, and having besieged Ctesiphon

blocks: and brought it to terms, hearing of the disasters of Asia, came in haste to Pontic Heraclea through Cappadocia with some of his forces, to catch the Scythians there; and he was treacherously killed by a man who was also named Odenathus. The Scythians had gone back to their own land by the same Pontus before he came; and his bodyguards destroyed Odenathus the murderer of Odenathus, and entrusted the rule of the East to Zenobia his wife.

Then also the Heruli, sailing with five hundred ships through Lake Maeotis to the Pontus, took Byzantium and Chrysopolis. There they gave battle and fell back a little to the mouth of the Euxine Pontus, the place called Hieron; and the next day, sailing down with a favourable wind, they put in first at the strait of Cyzicus, the greatest city of Bithynia, and then ravaged the islands of Lemnos and Scyros. And reaching Attica they set fire to Athens, and overran Corinth and Sparta and Argos and all Achaea, until the Athenians, ambushing them in some narrow places, killed very many of them; and the emperor Gallienus joined in, and killed three thousand by the Nestus. Then Naulobatus, leader of the Heruli, surrendered himself to the emperor Gallienus and was granted consular honour by him. And one Aureolus, a Celtic general of the Romans, treacherously killed Gallienus. So much for the emperors Valerian and Gallienus.

blocks: I will choose their delusions, and will repay them their sins." And having raged on in the kingship beyond his deserts, and being unable, with his crippled body, to put off the royal ornaments, he set up his two sons, who took on their father's sins. For in them the prophecy is plain which God spoke, "repaying the sins of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me." For laying on his sons' heads his own wicked desires, in which he failed, he wiped off on them his own evil and his hatred of God. So much the great Dionysius says about Valerian, and about Macrianus too.
Year of the world 5763. Year of the divine incarnation 263.

Claudius reigned as 27th emperor of Rome, one year. Claudius ruled one year. Under him too the Heruli fared badly, invading again with a host of ships in various places of the Romans' land; and they were hard pressed, now by sea battles, now by storms, now by famine, by which the same Claudius too was seized, and ended his life. After him Quintillus held power for all of 17 days, and died.

Aurelian reigned as 28th emperor of Rome, 6 years.
Aurelian subdued the Palmyrenes and brought Gaul under him; in his time, they say, Philostratus the Athenian historian and Longinus flourished.

Then Zenobia rose up against the Romans, gathering a very great force, and took control of Egypt, doing away with Probus, who was then the Romans' general there. Aurelian, not bearing this news, came with an army, and near Antioch in Syria, at a place called Immae, destroyed the Palmyrenes; and having captured Zenobia he brought her to Rome, and treating her with great kindness he married her honourably to a man of the senate. He also overcame the Gauls, who had risen then. And setting out against the Scythians too, he was done away with by his own army, falling into a mutiny between Byzantium and Heraclea, at the place called Caenophrurium in Thrace, when he was about to start a persecution against the Christians.

Uraraces reigned as 5th king of the Persians, 17 years.

Dionysius, bishop of Rome, 8 years. Domnus, 16th bishop of Antioch, 3 years. Cyrillus, bishop of Antioch, 15 years. Maximus, 15th bishop of Alexandria, 8 years. Mazabanes, 37th of Jerusalem, 21 years.
Year of the world 5765. Year of the divine incarnation 265.
Aurelian, already written of, 29th emperor of the Romans, 6 years.

In his 6th year Aurelian, about to start a persecution against the Christians, was prevented by a divine thunderbolt. And a plot being made against him by those around him, he was treacherously killed at Caenophrurium. After him Tacitus reigned 6 months. When he was slaughtered in Pontus, Florian was emperor 88 days. When he was slaughtered at Tarsus, Probus reigned 6 years, 4 months. Together they make 7 years.

blocks: Year of the world 5770. Year of the divine incarnation 270.

In the third year of Probus, Anatolius, bishop of Laodicea, became known as distinguished in the sciences of the philosophers. In the 4th year of Probus the ruin of the mad Manichaeans was brought into the life of men. In the 6th year of Probus, Saturninus, a commander of the army, began to build the new Antioch; afterwards he rose against the Romans' rule and was slaughtered at Apamea by his own men. Probus was slaughtered at Sirmium.
Carus, 30th emperor of the Romans, with his sons Carinus and Numerian, 2 years.
Year of the world 5777. Year of the divine incarnation 277.

In the first year of Carinus, when Numerian came to Antioch and wished to go into the church and spy out the Christians' mysteries, the holy Babylas stopped him, saying, "It is not lawful for you to see the Christians' mysteries, defiled as you are by the sacrifices to idols." And Numerian was angered and killed him.
